strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in existing benchmarks by proposing the first comprehensive evaluation of continual learning with user feedback for LLMs
Comprehensive benchmark design with 11 datasets spanning 3 domains, 2 languages, 4 task types, and 20k cases
Well-designed taxonomy of memory (declarative/procedural) and feedback (explicit/implicit) grounded in cognitive science and IR
Rigorous experimental setup with both off-policy and on-policy learning, multiple evaluation metrics, and thorough ablations
Excellent reproducibility with detailed 41-page appendix including complete prompts, hyperparameters, and promised code/data release
Important practical findings showing SOTA memory systems underperform naive RAG, with actionable efficiency analysis
User feedback simulation framework combining LLM-as-user paradigm with two-stage probabilistic action modeling
Clear validation that simulated feedback is beneficial for performance improvement (Section A.3.5)
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation: LLM-generated feedback may not reflect actual user preferences, especially for subjective tasks; limited validation beyond showing performance gains
Satisfaction→action conversion uses fixed sigmoid functions calibrated to specific studies (Shuster et al., Chatterji et al.); generalizability across user populations unclear
Evaluation metric aggregation issues: min-max normalization across datasets with varying score ranges can hide differences; choice between normalization strategies not well justified
Context truncation when exceeding model limits applied without systematic analysis of impact on results
Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests despite high variance in LLM outputs; Table 13 shows large fluctuations

Incomplete analysis of key findings: (1) why memory systems underperform RAG explanation is underdeveloped, (2) SiLo anomaly where Vanilla outperforms all memory systems receives minimal investigation, (3) performance fluctuations on specialized domains lack root cause analysis
On-policy experiments incomplete: many systems excluded due to computational constraints; Mem0 pathological slowdown (>20 min/entry) shown in Figure 10 but not deeply investigated
Limited generalizability: all user simulation uses Qwen-32B; backbone LLMs only Qwen3-8B (main) and Qwen3-32B (one experiment); potential data contamination from Qwen training not discussed
Primarily a benchmark resource without novel algorithmic contributions; limited advancement beyond applying existing IR techniques to LLMs
Presentation issues: circular Figure 2 harder to interpret; key implementation details scattered across 41-page appendix; some methodological choices unexplained

strengths: Addresses a relevant gap: existing benchmarks focus primarily on reading comprehension with long inputs/short outputs rather than evaluating continual learning from user feedback
Comprehensive scope: 20k cases across 11 datasets, 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 task types provides broad coverage
Well-motivated taxonomy grounded in neuroscience and IR literature for categorizing memory types and feedback types
Strong reproducibility practices: detailed experimental setup, promised open-sourcing of code and data, extensive appendices with ablation studies
Clear presentation: well-written with good use of examples, tables, and visualizations to explain the framework
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: memory taxonomy is from cognitive science (1968), feedback taxonomy from IR (50+ years), and LLM-as-user simulation from existing work. The contribution is primarily aggregative rather than innovative

Critical validity issue: entire evaluation relies on unvalidated LLM-simulated user feedback. No human evaluation demonstrates that simulated feedback resembles real user behavior patterns, undermining core findings

Incomplete on-policy experiments: some systems (Mem0) failed to complete due to extreme slowdown (>6 hours, manually terminated). On-policy learning is the most realistic continual learning setting, yet results are only partial

Shallow analysis of main findings: the negative result (memory systems underperform RAG) lacks deep investigation. The proposed explanation that 'memory systems don't differentiate task logs from feedback' is diagnostic but not prescriptive—no solutions are proposed

Unfair experimental setup: Vanilla baseline receives full context window for static knowledge datasets while memory systems retrieve only 5 entries; context truncation uses simple cutting that could bias results

Methodological concerns: small test sets (often <100 instances from some datasets), arbitrary thresholds (600-token boundary), no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. Task diversity limited to text generation variants

Incomplete baseline evaluation: uses released code with default settings for A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS without domain-specific tuning, making it unclear whether poor performance reflects fundamental limitations or suboptimal configurations

Efficiency disparities unaddressed: MemoryOS takes 17-21 seconds per case for memory operations vs. 0.02 seconds for BM25, and Mem0 exhibits pathological slowdown. Benchmark fairness to systems with high overhead is questionable

Performance on individual datasets contradicts conclusions: memory systems outperform RAG on Locomo (acknowledged in paper), suggesting negative finding may be artifact of task diversity rather than fundamental limitation
Heavy reliance on LLM-as-Judge for evaluation: uses LLM to merge multiple metrics, introducing additional bias with no validation that aggregation reflects actual quality

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: First comprehensive benchmark combining multiple memory types (declarative/procedural) and feedback types (explicit/implicit) for evaluating continual learning in LLMs with user feedback
Comprehensive scope with 20k cases across 11 datasets, 3 domains, 2 languages, and diverse task formats - provides robust evaluation platform
Well-motivated taxonomy grounded in neuroscience and IR literature providing principled framework for organizing evaluation dimensions
Valuable negative results showing SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) often underperform naive RAG baselines, challenging the field and motivating better algorithms
Thoughtful hybrid feedback simulation combining metric-based evaluation for objective tasks and LLM-as-user for subjective tasks with probabilistic action modeling grounded in empirical user studies
Excellent reproducibility with open-sourced code, baselines, pre-generated feedback logs, detailed prompts, and multiple experimental settings (off-policy, on-policy, stepwise)
Thorough experiments with ablations validating feedback quality (Tables 11-13) and comprehensive analysis of time consumption and efficiency trade-offs
weaknesses: Limited analysis of root causes: Paper identifies that memory systems 'do not differentiate task context from feedback logs' but lacks deep investigation, ablation studies of memory components, or testing of simple fixes to address this fundamental issue

LLM-based evaluation introduces noise and potential biases: User simulator quality depends on Qwen-32B, LLM-as-judge adds variance for metric integration, and fixed sigmoid hyperparameters (S₀L=7.5, kL=1.5) may not generalize across domains - no inter-rater reliability analysis provided

Context truncation ('simply cutting context to fit') when inputs exceed limits could introduce artifacts; deterministic sigmoid mapping to user actions may not be correct model; metric aggregation via min-max/z-score may obscure important differences

Missing investigation of key puzzles: Why does Vanilla outperform memory systems on SiLo? Why do performance fluctuations occur during training on Academic/Legal domains? Why does feedback sometimes not help or decrease performance (Table 11)?

No actionable insights for practitioners: Paper identifies problems but doesn't propose solutions or conduct experiments testing fixes; doesn't discuss implications for future system design or architecture

Benchmark complexity may limit adoption: 11 datasets with different metrics requiring integration, different evaluation paths, external dependencies (Qwen models, embeddings) that may change; difficult to extend or adapt

Modest feedback effect sizes: Table 11 shows improvements sometimes marginal or negative; Table 13 shows memory systems sometimes underperform Vanilla; no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals reported

Presentation could be more focused: 41 pages is very dense; key findings buried (context differentiation issue mentioned briefly); Figure 2 radial plot hard to parse; could better summarize implications

strengths: Addresses important gap in LLM benchmarking by providing first comprehensive benchmark for memory and continual learning with user feedback
Comprehensive benchmark design with well-motivated taxonomies grounded in neuroscience and IR literature, covering 3 domains, 2 languages, 4 task formats, and 20k cases
Sophisticated user feedback simulation using multi-path architecture combining metric-based and LLM-as-user approaches with probabilistic action modeling
Thorough experimental evaluation across 8 LLMsys with on-policy/off-policy settings, time consumption analysis, and robustness studies (noisy feedback, different backbones)
Excellent reproducibility with open-sourced code, data, and detailed appendix with implementation details and prompt templates
Valuable findings revealing SOTA memory systems underperform naive RAG baselines and struggle with procedural memory utilization
Human annotation validation showing LLM-generated feedback is largely indistinguishable from human-written feedback (59% win-rate on quality)
weaknesses: Moderate feedback simulation quality with low inter-annotator agreement on naturalness (Kappa 0.093) suggesting simulated feedback may systematically differ from real user behavior
Puzzling experimental results where all methods including SOTA underperform naive baselines need stronger interpretation—raises questions about benchmark fairness vs. system limitations
Context truncation when inputs exceed limits may unfairly penalize SOTA systems not designed for such constraints; Mem0 excluded from experiments due to slowdown
Limited methodological novelty as memory and feedback taxonomies are largely borrowed from existing literature; primary contribution is benchmark creation rather than novel methods
LLM-as-Judge merging multiple metrics introduces additional judgment layer; metric aggregation via normalization/z-scoring may obscure important task-specific differences
Procedural memory definition is loose and unclear how well datasets labeled as procedural actually test procedural knowledge or how user feedback trains this specifically
On-policy and stepwise off-policy results show highly volatile performance with unexplained fluctuations; performance sometimes decreases with accumulated feedback without clear analysis
Heavy emphasis on reading comprehension tasks (LiSo dominates); imbalanced dataset sizes after subsampling; unclear generalization beyond Qwen family models
Limited guidance for practitioners and algorithm designers on which methods to use or how to build better systems; benchmark reveals problems but offers limited solutions

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in LLM benchmarking - existing benchmarks focus on static long-context tasks rather than continual learning from accumulated feedback
Comprehensive scope with 11 datasets across 3 domains, 2 languages, 4 task formats, and 20k cases with diverse characteristics
Well-motivated taxonomy of memory types (declarative/procedural, semantic/episodic) and feedback types grounded in neuroscience and IR literature
Thoughtful three-module architecture (Task Provider, User Simulator, Performance Monitor) combining metric-based and LLM-based evaluation
Strong reproducibility: extensive open-sourcing of code, scripts, prompts, pre-generated feedback logs, and detailed experimental protocols
Human validation of feedback quality with pairwise annotation study comparing simulated vs. human-written feedback
weaknesses: Disappointing experimental findings undermine core motivation: SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) systematically underperform simple RAG baselines, with limited deep analysis of why or guidance on building better systems

User simulation quality concerns: low inter-rater reliability (Fleiss' Kappa 0.093-0.38), marginal preference for simulated feedback (50-59.5%), and probabilistic model calibrated on limited user studies; unclear if results transfer to real user behavior

Experimental design biases against complex systems: on-policy experiments abandoned because some systems are 'too slow'; Mem0 completely fails on DialSim (runs 12+ hours without completing); benchmark implicitly rewards speed over capability

Inadequate analysis of failure modes: SiLo paradox (Vanilla beats all memory systems) receives minimal investigation; single case study; no systematic ablations; procedural vs. declarative memory distinction is intuitive but weakly supported

Metric aggregation obscures findings: merging diverse metrics (ROUGE-L, F1, Accuracy, LLM-as-Judge) through min-max/z-score normalization and additional LLM evaluation creates potential circularity and masks specific capability weaknesses

Generalizability concerns: results based entirely on LLM-simulated feedback, not real users; all tests use Qwen3/Mistral models; potential circular dependency (LLMs evaluating LLMs); unclear if findings transfer to actual deployment

Limited novelty and actionability: benchmark-only contribution with no new methods or insights into building better systems; taxonomy and LLM-as-user paradigm are established; main finding ('existing systems insufficient') lacks guidance for improvement
Performance instability: acknowledged significant fluctuations during training especially on Academic/Legal domains (A.3.7); large error bars (Tables 13-14) raise reliability questions
Truncated long contexts treated equally across systems: different systems have different context limits; truncation to fit may artificially penalize methods designed for long contexts

Dataset and task imbalance: LiSo dominates (1250 samples) vs. SiSo/SiLo (713/750); some subsets too small (82-213 samples) for robust conclusions; even sampling doesn't address task difficulty differences

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark addressing genuine gap in memory/continual learning evaluation for LLMs, with principled taxonomies grounded in neuroscience and IR literature

Excellent execution and reproducibility: heterogeneous datasets across 3 domains/languages, well-designed LLM-as-user feedback simulation framework with human validation, open-sourced code/data/feedback logs

Important empirical findings revealing that SOTA memory systems (Mem0, MemoryOS, A-Mem) frequently underperform simple RAG baselines, with identified efficiency issues and weak procedural memory utilization
Extensive, rigorous experimental coverage: on/off-policy settings, multiple backbones, detailed hyperparameter documentation, investigation of edge cases (e.g., Mem0 pathological slowdown)
High-quality presentation with clear writing, effective visualizations, and comprehensive appendix enabling reproduction
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: memory taxonomies follow established neuroscience frameworks (Atkinson & Shiffrin 1968), feedback taxonomy from 50+ years of IR research, LLM-as-user not new; primary contribution is integration into benchmark rather than novel methodology

Insufficient analysis of key findings: striking underperformance of SOTA methods deserves deeper investigation; procedural vs. declarative memory explanation (Section 3.3) is speculative; lacks systematic ablations to isolate failure factors; case study (Table 23) provides limited mechanistic insight

Evaluation methodology concerns: low inter-annotator agreement on feedback quality (Kappa 0.093-0.380 despite 50-59% similarity), only 200/20k cases human-annotated, LLM-as-Judge introduces additional bias layer, min-max normalization across diverse datasets questionable, unclear dataset imbalance handling

Experimental design limitations: off-policy setting with pre-generated feedback less challenging than true online learning; some baselines excluded due to computational constraints (Mem0 on Open-Domain); context truncation may unfairly disadvantage methods; only 3 interaction turns tested vs. true continual learning with concept drift

Feedback simulation limitations: single persona per dataset, heavy Qwen-32B dependency (generalization unclear despite partial validation), deterministic action mapping, under-explored implicit feedback, noisy feedback experiments limited in scope

Missing depth on failure modes: why are memory mechanisms ineffective for procedural learning? No ablations on memory components, no task characteristic analysis favoring memory vs. retrieval, no investigation of alternative training paradigms (fine-tuning, prompt engineering)
Statistical analysis gaps: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis across runs; inconsistent standard deviation reporting

Feedback utility question: Table 16 shows modest with-vs-without feedback gains (0.01-0.13 for most datasets), raising whether simulated feedback genuinely trains systems or optimizes for LLM-as-Judge evaluation
